content: Telemedicine (TM) refers to the use of telecommunication systems to provide healthcare services remotely. It has the potential to enhance patient health outcomes, improve access to healthcare, and reduce costs. As telemedicine applications continue to evolve, it is crucial to evaluate their impact on patients, healthcare professionals, and the organization of care. The objective of this study was to assess the effectiveness, acceptability, and costs of interactive telemedicine as an alternative to, or in addition to, traditional care methods such as face-to-face consultations or telephone consultations. The study included randomized controlled trials that involved direct interaction between patients and healthcare providers through telemedicine, either as a substitute for or in addition to usual care. Interventions that relied solely on telephone communication or fully automated self-management systems were excluded. A total of 93 trials, involving 22,047 participants, were included in the analysis. These trials evaluated the use of interactive telemedicine in various clinical conditions, including cardiovascular disease, diabetes, respiratory conditions, mental health or substance abuse disorders, and others. Telemedicine interventions included remote monitoring and real-time video conferencing, either used alone or in combination. The primary functions of telemedicine varied depending on the clinical condition and included chronic condition monitoring, treatment or rehabilitation delivery, self-management education, specialist consultations, real-time clinical assessments, and screening. For patients with heart failure, telemedicine showed no significant difference in all-cause mortality compared to usual care over a median follow-up of six months. Hospital admissions varied widely, with some studies reporting a decrease of up to 64% and others reporting an increase of up to 60% over a median follow-up of eight months. There was moderate evidence suggesting improved quality of life for telemedicine users compared to usual care at a median follow-up of three months. In patients with diabetes, telemedicine was associated with a significant reduction in glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) levels over a median follow-up of nine months. There was also evidence of reductions in low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol levels and blood pressure (both systolic and diastolic) in telemedicine users compared to those receiving usual care. For mental health and substance abuse conditions, no significant differences were observed between therapy delivered via video conferencing and face-to-face therapy. The findings suggest that telemedicine can achieve similar health outcomes to traditional care for certain conditions, such as heart failure, and may improve specific clinical parameters, such as blood glucose control in diabetes. However, the cost-effectiveness and acceptability of telemedicine remain unclear due to limited data. The effectiveness of telemedicine likely depends on factors such as the severity and trajectory of the condition, the purpose of the intervention (e.g., monitoring or diagnostic services), and the healthcare system and providers involved in its delivery.
